subject: pufferfish
reasoning:
I'm figuring out the setup for a pufferfish model in three.js — a single TypeScript module built from primitives, using meters and standard orientation, deciding whether it should rest on the ground plane or float as a display piece.

Since the pitch doesn't call for flight, I'll have it rest on the sea floor at y≈0. I'm thinking through real-world scale (roughly 0.3m long) and the anatomy to build: a rounded inflated body with pectoral/dorsal/anal/caudal fins, a small beak-like mouth, big eyes, and spines, using a scaled sphere for the body plus a lighter belly shape and a yellow-olive color scheme with spots.

Writing sphere geometry parameters...

For the spines, I'll distribute them using a Fibonacci sphere pattern on the ellipsoid's surface, computing outward normals from the gradient and orienting each cone to face away from center, while avoiding the face region. I'll use InstancedMesh with a single geometry and material for efficiency across roughly 150 spine instances, since that's available in three's core without needing extra utility imports.

For the eyes, I'm placing large bulging white spheres with dark pupils on the upper front sides of the body to give that classic pufferfish look, and for the mouth I'm sketching a small beak-like shape from simple cone or box geometry in a darker tone with a pale tooth accent, keeping the forms low-poly and simple.

For the fins, I'm planning thin fan-shaped pectoral fins made from flat custom Shape outlines rendered double-sided, angled outward near the lower head, plus small dorsal and anal fins and a fanned tail fin at the back since the body faces forward. I'm also considering flattening the body slightly, scaling it narrower in width and height than its length for a more stylized pufferfish silhouette.

I'm sizing the body to roughly 0.27-0.36m total including tail, and figuring out how to rest it on the floor by computing a bounding box and shifting the whole group up so its lowest point touches y=0, though I'm wary that Box3's handling of instanced meshes might not work reliably, so I may need to calculate the belly's lowest point analytically instead.

I'm deciding to set the body's center height so the bottom sits right at the floor (perhaps sinking in slightly, within the allowed 2% margin), while making sure fins stay above that line, and considering whether the pose should be neutral with fins extended for visual interest.

For colors, I'm picking an olive-yellow body with dark brown spots, white belly, cream-tipped spines, large eyes with white/black/orange detailing, a small dark beak mouth, and translucent orange fins using semi-transparent material. I'm planning to scatter roughly 25 flattened disc-shaped spots across the body using an instanced mesh, and considering a canvas-drawn texture to add a pale belly gradient alongside the spots.

I'm weighing whether a canvas texture would map well onto the sphere's UV coordinates — painting olive at the top fading to cream at the bottom should align naturally with how three.js orients sphere UVs, though spots near the poles would stretch unevenly. It's a reasonable approach despite the seam and pole compression concerns, so I'll lean toward using it for the gradient and spot pattern.

I decide canvas texture support needs a guard against environments without `document`, falling back gracefully if unavailable. For the actual spot pattern though, I'm now considering 3D instanced discs instead of canvas-painted spots for better control, paired with either a canvas gradient or vertex colors for the belly-to-back color transition.

Thinking through vertex colors versus two overlapping meshes for the olive-to-cream gradient: vertex colors give a smooth but blocky transition depending on polygon density, while a separate cream belly cap mesh gives a crisp stylized edge but risks z-fighting since it shares the same sphere surface. I'd need to either slightly offset the belly cap's radius outward or use polygon offset to avoid flickering at the seam, treating the boundary as a raised belly plate for a puppet-like look.

I decide to go with a belly cap mesh using polygon offset rather than vertex colors, and start sketching out the body proportions as a scaled sphere with separate half-width, half-height, and half-length radii, positioning its center so the bottom sits at ground level.

Now I'm working out segment counts for the body—opting for a moderately smooth 24x16 since it's the main shape—and figuring out the mouth and beak placement near the front tip of the ellipsoid, planning small sphere or cone shapes for the upper dark beak and lower cream plate to give it that pufferfish beak look.

For the color palette, I'm settling on a mustard-yellow/olive back, cream belly, dark brown spots, cream spines, white eyes with black pupils, orange translucent fins and tail, and a dark brown beak with cream teeth, landing on roughly nine materials total.

Now I'm working out spine placement using instanced cone geometry, sampling around 220 points via Fibonacci sphere distribution, skipping the front mouth/eye region, the tail area, and the very underside so the fish doesn't look spiky where it rests on the floor.

For eyes, I'm placing them near the front-top sides and making sure spines avoid that zone by checking directional distance to the eye positions. Then I'm setting up spots using small flattened cylinder discs scattered across the upper body with varied sizes, using a seeded random generator for consistent placement, and writing the Fibonacci sphere sampling logic to distribute points evenly across the body.

Now I'm detailing eye construction: computing the outward normal at the eye direction to position a protruding eyeball sphere, then placing a darker pupil sphere offset along that normal so it pokes out slightly, plus a tiny white highlight sphere for shine.

I'm working out eye placement coordinates, confirming left/right symmetry, then moving on to the pectoral fins, which sit behind the eyes on the body sides and extend outward and backward as flattened paddle shapes oriented somewhat vertically to flap sideways like real puffers.

Actually I'll orient the fin so its flat face points sideways like a visible fan from the side, matching pufferfish reference images, with the fan extending backward from the body. I'm working out the rotation math to map the flat shape geometry's local axes onto the correct world directions so the fin reads correctly in 3D.

For the tail fin, I'm reasoning that it should sit vertically in the sagittal plane (the plane containing body length and height), with its normal pointing along the width axis, consistent with how a real fish tail fin is oriented.

I'm applying the same logic to the pectoral, dorsal, and anal fins: pectoral fins match the tail's orientation, the dorsal fin sits atop the body near the tail as a small rounded fan, and the anal fin sits below near the tail, positioned carefully so it doesn't dip below the floor given the body's curved underside.

Now I'm shaping the caudal fin and peduncle: a short cylindrical stalk connects the body's rear to the tail fin, and I'm defining the tail fin as a symmetric rounded fan shape spanning from the peduncle base outward to curved tips above and below.

Working out the fin coordinate mapping...

For pectoral fins I want them angled outward from the body sides, so I'm considering a slight rotation on the Z axis to make them flare naturally. I'll keep the fin material simple—translucent orange with double-sided rendering—and skip extra details like fan rays or stripes to avoid overcomplicating the shape.

For character, I want expressive big eyes with dark pupils, and I'm adding a subtle dark gill slit behind each eye using a small torus arc rotated to curve against the body's side, giving it a believable puffer-fish texture without overdoing it.

Now I'm working out the mouth — a cone pair forming a beak shape pointing forward at the front of the body, positioned between the eyes with the tip extending slightly past the head. I settle on simple cone and box geometry for upper and lower beak plates, then check overall proportions: total body length around 0.36m from tail tip to beak front, with height roughly 0.22.

I'm comparing against a real pufferfish, settling on about 0.3m total length and confirming my 0.32m model is close enough. I position the body so its bottom rests exactly on the floor at y=0, verify the fins and spines clear the ground, and then adjust the tail's vertical position since it was sitting a bit too high — lowering the tail center to bring its underside closer to the floor like a real fish.

Now I'm working out the peduncle (the tapered connector between body and tail), figuring out the cylinder geometry and rotation math so it's wider near the body and narrower toward the tail, then placing the tail fin group at the correct offset to attach smoothly at the back.

For the dorsal fin, I'm calculating where the body's top curve sits at the relevant z-position, then sketching a fin shape with a curved peak using quadratic bezier points so its base sits flush against the body's back.

Working through the dorsal fin geometry a bit more, I settle on a base height around 0.16 with a peak around 0.075 above it, giving a visible tip that pokes a few centimeters above the body surface near the back — a reasonably proportioned small pufferfish fin. That seems good enough to move forward with.

For the anal fin, I check that its base sits inside the body near the bottom rear, with the shape curving downward and backward so the visible portion stays above the floor level once positioned. I decide a second lower fin pair isn't necessary.

For the pectoral fins, I'm positioning them vertically against the body's sides, computing where the surface sits at that x-coordinate so the fin base aligns with the body surface before it extends backward and outward.

I'm sketching the pectoral fin as a small paddle shape with curved edges, then tilting each fin outward by rotating around the Z-axis—negative for one side, positive for the mirrored side—so the top edge leans away from the body.

Now I'm placing scattered dark spots across the back using an irregular Fibonacci-like distribution, avoiding the eye region, with each spot as a thin cylinder oriented to the body's surface normal and randomly scaled for a natural, uneven look.

For spines, I'm using small low-poly cones angled outward from the surface normal, distributing roughly 200 of them with density excluding areas too close to the eyes, the front mouth region, and the tail peduncle so the spikes read as a stylized textured pattern rather than uniform coverage.

For the eyes I'm keeping it simple: a white sphere base, dark pupil sphere, and tiny highlight dot, skipping any eyelid detail since bulging eyes suit the puffer look better. For the belly, I'm carving a cream-colored cap using a partial sphere geometry so the lighter underside blends naturally into the body color around the lower third of the form.

I'm refining the belly cap math — scaling it slightly larger than the body (about 1.2%) so its edge sits just outside the surface and avoids z-fighting without needing polygon offset, accepting a tiny near-invisible lip at the boundary.

Now I'm settling material colors for each body part — mustard body, pale cream belly, dark spots, light spines, orange translucent fins, dark beak and pale teeth — along with the pupil and eye-white tones, then setting up the metadata object and a seeded RNG before writing the actual TypeScript module code.

Still placing spines...

Setting up spot geometry now...

I'll tighten the dy threshold to -0.1 to keep spots clear of the belly boundary. For the eyes, I'm computing eye and pupil placement as small spheres offset along the surface normal so they bulge slightly outward, sizing the pupil radius so it sits flush on the eyeball rather than poking past its surface.

I'm layering in an orange iris sphere between the eyeball and pupil, plus a tiny highlight dot, offsetting each slightly along the normal so the eye reads as a cute, stylized big round eye rather than a flat dot.

Checking that the fin positions sit correctly relative to the eye and body surface, then shaping the dorsal fin with its own curved outline, rotating it to point backward, and working out its vertical placement so the peak rises above the body's curved profile near the front-to-back midpoint.

For the tail, I'm designing a rounded fan shape with a trailing edge that bulges outward then back in, forming the classic puffer fish caudal fin, and then working out its placement along the z-axis so the peduncle and tail base line up properly without making the total body length too long.

For the mouth, I'm placing a small cone as the upper beak, rotated so its tip points forward, calculating its position so it protrudes just slightly past the body's front surface at the right height. Then I assemble the whole mesh inside a group and return it as the final model, double-checking that key features sit at consistent heights — making sure the body bottom rests at zero, spines and fins clear the ground, and the belly cap sinks only a negligible amount — so the overall proportions hold together correctly.
